newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russian market welcomes Norilsk tender.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russian market welcomes Norilsk tender.

text.p: The sale of a controlling stake in Russian mining giant Norilsk Nickel was given a warm welcome by equity and metal analysts on Wednesday.

The sale, under threat until the very last minute because of objections by senior government figures, eventually went ahead as planned and was won late on Tuesday by a firm representing powerful commercial bank Uneximbank.
The possibility of the controversial deal being derailed had unsettled investors, and news of the auction was greeted with a sigh of relief.
"Because the company now has an owner, this means that people will invest money in the company," said Alexei Labovsky, metals analyst with CentreInvest Securities in Moscow.

Uneximbank had control of the 38 percent stake, representing 51 percent of voting shares, since late 1995, and its victory in the tender should provide management and restructuring continuity for the troubled group, analysts said.

"This result was a good one for Norilsk, because Uneximbank had started the restructuring process in 1996, and it was generally positive for the company," said Boris Chernak, metals analyst at ING-Barings in Moscow.
Share prices also reacted positively to the tender outcome. Results of the Norilsk sale were announced after the Russian Trading System had closed on Tuesday.
Ordinary shares in RAO Norilsky Nikel firmed to $15.50 on Wednesday from $15.15. Preferred shares rose to $13.50 from $12.60.
Norilsk, vying to become the world's biggest nickel producer this year, is the top supplier of precious metal palladium and a major producer of copper, platinum and cobalt.

Its vast mining and processing operations are profitable, but the company has accumulated huge debts, partly because it shoulders the burden of supporting the entire Arctic city of Norilsk, where its main production plant is based.

Norilsk estimates that the group supports 500,000 people, but its workforce is less than 150,000. Analysts said they expected Uneximbank to continue to negotiate the transfer of social costs to local authorities.
Uneximbank has succeeded in restructuring around half the group's debts, and has pushed through production increases in 1997 that few would have thought possible two years ago.
The bank paid a total of around $620 million for its successful bid -- $250 million for the shares, $300 million to develop a gas deposit, and around $70 million to pay off debts.
Development of its own gas field was viewed as crucial to the success of the company, because Norilsk depends heavily on gas from Norilskgazprom to fuel its flagship metals combine.
The faster Norilsk develops an independent source of energy the better, particularly because its relations with Norilskgazprom are far from smooth, analysts said.
The final price tag at the auction was cheap based on Norilsk's recent share performance, they added.

"Effectively, Uneximbank paid $12.85 per share, approximately 15 percent below the current market value," Creditanstalt Investment Bank Russia said in a report, referring to Tuesday's closing share price of $15.15.
The medium to long term outlook for the company and its shares was bullish, because it could now enjoy the fruits of Uneximbank's restructuring plans.
However, plans to issue 126 million ordinary shares in a rights issue could dent share value in the short term.

"In September there will probably be a share issue, and so shares may well go down to $9-10, but we are recommending people hold on to their shares and subscribe to the issue, because we believe the market will go up eventually," Chernak said.
The issue plan includes setting a price of around $5.20 on the new shares. Norilsk management has also put forward a proposal to convert all preferred shares into ordinaries.
